prompt: What is an express building permit and do I qualify?
answer:
An Express Building Permit is an enhanced service for smaller, less complex projects that aims to review eligible applications within 3 business days after intake. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-review-streams/]

You may qualify for Express Services if your project falls into one of these categories:

**Small Residential Projects:**
- Part 9 houses with not more than two dwelling units (no active permits for new buildings/additions)
- Detached ancillary structures (garages, carports, sheds)
- Decks and porches
- Interior alterations
- Basement walkouts and underpinning
- Work impacting party walls (with enhanced requirements)
- Minor fire damage repair
- 1 to 2 unit conversions (max 2 units per building)
- Stand-alone plumbing and drain permits
- Solar panel installations attached to existing buildings

**Small Commercial Projects:**
- Interior alterations to Assembly/Industrial occupancies (up to 300m², no change in use/patron area)
- Interior alterations to Business/Office/Retail/Restaurants with <30 seats (up to 600m², no change in use/patron area)
- Tents (including certified tents)
- Minor fire damage repair
- Stand-alone maglocks
- Solar panel installations attached to existing buildings

**Sign Permits:**
- First Party Signs (up to 3 signs)
- Third Party Signs (up to 3 signs)

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

Projects that do NOT qualify include additions to residential dwellings, laneway/garden suites, properties requiring Heritage Approval, attached garages/carports, master plan sign applications, variances, and sign permits for more than three signs. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

prompt: What is an express building permit and do I qualify?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, an Express Building Permit is an enhanced service for smaller, less complex projects with a predefined scope. Toronto Building's goal is to review eligible applications within **3 business days** after the permit has been taken in. **To qualify, your project must be one of the following types:**

**Small Residential Projects:**
*   For a Part 9 house with not more than two dwelling units and no active permit for a new building or addition.
*   Detached residential ancillary structures (garages, carports, sheds).
*   Decks and porches.
*   Interior alterations.
*   Basement walkouts and underpinning.
*   Work impacting a party wall (with enhanced submission requirements).
*   Minor fire damage repair.
*   1 to 2 unit conversions (no more than 2 unit dwellings per building).
*   Stand-alone plumbing and drain permits.
*   Solar panel installations attached to an existing building.

**Small Commercial Projects:**
*   Interior alterations to Assembly and Industrial occupancies (Group A & F) up to 300 sq. m, with no change in use or patron area, and no active building shell permit.
*   Interior alterations to Business, Office, Retail, and Restaurants with <30 seats (Group D & E) up to 600 sq. m, with no change in use or patron area, and no active building shell permit.
*   Tents (including certified tents).
*   Minor fire damage repair.
*   Stand-alone maglocks.
*   Solar panel installations attached to an existing building.

**Solar Panels:**
*   All building-mounted stand-alone solar panels.

**Sign Permits:**
*   First Party Signs (up to 3 signs).
*   Third Party Signs (up to 3 signs).

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

**Projects that do NOT qualify for Express Services include:**
*   Additions to residential dwellings, laneway suites, and garden suites.
*   Projects requiring Heritage Approval.
*   Attached garages and carports.
*   Sign applications for master plans, variances, or for more than three signs.
*   Revisions to permits for work outside the Express Services scope.

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

**How to apply:**
*   For specific stand-alone residential projects (detached carports, garages, decks, porches, ancillary structures), apply via the **online application portal**.
*   For all other small residential and commercial Express Services projects, apply via email to **bldapplications@toronto.ca**.
*   For all sign permit applications, apply via email to **expressservices@toronto.ca**.

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

To determine if you qualify, compare your specific project to the lists above. For further information, you can contact **ExpressServices@toronto.ca**. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

prompt: What inspections are required during construction in Toronto?
answer:
During construction in Toronto, various mandatory inspections are required to ensure compliance with the Building Code Act and the issued building and demolition permits. The specific inspections required depend on the nature of the project.

For small buildings (Part 9 of the Ontario Building Code including houses and small commercial structures), the inspections required include:

1. Footing formwork and reinforcement before pouring concrete
2. Foundation weeping tile and damp-proofing before backfilling
3. Foundation wall before backfilling
4. Drain, waste, and vent rough-in before insulation
5. Water service and backflow preventer before insulation
6. Sewer service lateral before insulation
7. Structural framing before insulation
8. Insulation and vapour/air barrier before interior finishes
9. Fire separation
10. Final interior and exterior inspection

For large buildings (Part 3 of the Ontario Building Code), the inspections required include:

1. Footings at completion of formwork, before pouring concrete
2. Foundations at completion
3. Structural framing at completion of structural framing for each storey
4. Fire separations and closures at completion of framing for wall, floor ad shaft fire separations including closures, continuity and fire stopping and before applying the interior finishes, spray fireproofing and lay-in tiles to ceilings
5. Insulation and vapour/air barrier at completion of insulation & vapour/air barrier and before installation of interior services
6. Fireplaces, gas appliances, and chimneys at commencement of installation
7. Life safety systems at completion of rough-in of the safety systems - referral to Toronto Fire Prevention
8. Occupancy (consult your inspector)
9. Final interior inspection at completion of interior construction, life safety systems and all fire separations and enclosures
10. Final exterior inspection at completion of grading, exterior finishes, fire routes, parking, hydrants and site amenities

For plumbing inspections, the required inspections include:

1. Site Meeting at start of construction, special systems such as pools, window washing etc. should be discussed
2. Outside storm & sanitary sewers at completion, before back filling and ready for testing
3. Water service at completion, before back filling and ready for testing
4. Inside storm & sanitary sewers at completion, could be partial, ready for testing
5. Rough-in, water supply, drains, waste & vents at completion and ready for testing
6. Occupancy at completion of installation of all required fixtures
7. Final inspection at completion of installation of remaining fixtures
8. Final exterior inspection at completion of grading, exterior finishes, fire routes, parking, hydrants and site amenities

prompt: How much does a residential building permit cost in Toronto?
answer:
The cost of a residential building permit in Toronto is **not a single flat fee** – it is calculated based on the type of work you are doing and the floor‑area involved. The city applies a **minimum fee of $214.79 (2026 rates)** to every permit application, and then adds a charge that is expressed as a **Service Index (SI) per square metre** for the specific work.

**How the fee is worked out**

| Type of residential work | How the fee is calculated |
|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| **New house (including decks, fireplaces, porches)** | Fee = SI × Floor‑area (m²). The SI is a dollar amount per square metre that varies by occupancy and work type. |
| **Addition to an existing house** | Same as a new house – fee is based on the floor area of the addition (SI × m²). |
| **New deck, fireplace, or detached garage** | Charged a **flat fee** (size does not affect the amount). |
| **Finished basement** | Charged per square metre of the finished area (SI × m²). |
| **Interior alterations – residential occupancies (e.g., floor replacement)** | Service Index shown as **$13.41 per m²** of proposed work. |
| **All other residential work** | The city’s fee schedule (available on the Building Fees page) provides the appropriate SI for each classification. |

**Key points**

* **Minimum fee:** Every residential permit must include at least **$214.79** before any other calculations are applied. [Source: “Minimum fee of $214.79 (2026) shall be charged for all work.”]  
* **No permit is issued until all fees are paid.** [Source: “No permit will be issued until all fees are paid.”]  
* **Payment options:** Fees can be paid by cash, cheque, debit card, Visa or MasterCard (Visa/MasterCard limited to $20,000). [Source: “Accepted Methods of Payment & Limits”]  

Because the Service Index varies by the specific classification of the residential work (new house, addition, basement, etc.), the exact dollar amount for a permit can only be determined after you know the **type of work and the total floor area** involved. You can view the complete list of Service Index rates on the City’s **Building Fees** page (toronto.ca/building-fees). [Source: “A list of all of the fees can be found at toronto.ca/building-fees.”]  

**Bottom line:**  
A residential building permit starts at a **minimum of $214.79** and then adds a per‑square‑metre charge (e.g., $13.41 /m² for floor replacement) or a flat fee, depending on the work. To get the precise cost for your project, you’ll need to identify the work classification and calculate the fee using the applicable Service Index and your project’s floor‑area.

   * **Zoning Review** – checks compliance with the Zoning By‑law (land use, building size, setbacks, parking, height, etc.) and other statutes (Conservation Authorities Act, Planning Act, etc.). [Source: Plan Review Process – Zoning Review]

prompt: What inspections are required during construction in Toronto?
answer:
In Toronto, any construction that is covered by a building permit must go through a series of **mandatory inspections** that are required by the Ontario Building Code. You (or your contractor) are responsible for notifying Toronto Building when the work is ready for each inspection; the cost of these inspections is already included in your permit fee. The inspector must be able to see the work being inspected, and a full‑scale coloured set of the stamped permit drawings must be on‑site for every visit【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/】.

### Typical inspections for **large‑building projects** (Part 3 of the Ontario Building Code)

| Inspection type | When to call for the inspection |
|-----------------|----------------------------------|
| **Footings** | At completion of formwork, before pouring concrete |
| **Foundations** | At completion of the foundation work |
| **Structural framing** | At completion of structural framing for each storey |
| **Fire separations and closures** | After framing of walls/floors/shafts, before interior finishes, spray fire‑proofing or ceiling tiles |
| **Insulation and vapour/air barrier** | After insulation & vapour barrier are installed, before interior services |
| **Fireplaces, gas appliances, and chimneys** | At the start of their installation |
| **Life‑safety systems** | After rough‑in of the systems (refer to Toronto Fire Prevention) |
| **Occupancy** | Consult your inspector (typically after all safety systems are in place) |
| **Final interior inspection** | After interior construction, life‑safety systems and all fire separations/enclosures are complete |
| **Final exterior inspection** | After grading, exterior finishes, fire routes, parking, hydrants and site amenities are complete |

### Typical **plumbing inspections** for large projects

| Inspection type | When to call |
|-----------------|--------------|
| **Site meeting** | At the start of construction (to discuss special systems such as pools, window‑washing, etc.) |
| **Outside storm & sanitary sewers** | At completion, before back‑filling and ready for testing |
| **Water service** | At completion, before back‑filling and ready for testing |
| **Inside storm & sanitary sewers** | At completion (may be partial), ready for testing |
| **Rough‑in, water supply, drains, waste & vents** | At completion and ready for testing |
| **Occupancy (plumbing)** | After installation of all required fixtures |
| **Final plumbing inspection** | After installation of any remaining fixtures |
| **Final exterior plumbing inspection** | After grading, exterior finishes, fire routes, parking, hydrants and site amenities |

### How to schedule the inspections

* **Request an inspection** through the Toronto Building online portal (or by phone) – you can book a date up to four weeks in advance, and the inspector will contact you to confirm the visit【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/】.  
* Inspections are performed **Monday‑Friday, 8:30 a.m. – 4:30 p.m.** (excluding statutory holidays)【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/】.  
* The inspector must be able to see the entire building element being inspected; any covered work must be uncovered before the inspection【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/when-to-call-for-inspection-of-large-buildings/】.  

### Other important points

* **Additional inspections** (beyond the mandatory ones) can be arranged through your local inspection office, but an extra fee may apply【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/】.  
* Failure to obtain the required inspections can cause **delays, work stoppages, and may lead to enforcement actions**【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/】.  

In summary, Toronto requires a series of staged, mandatory inspections—covering structural, fire‑safety, life‑safety, and plumbing elements—at specific points throughout construction. You must request each inspection when the work reaches the appropriate stage, have the permit drawings on site, and ensure the inspector can fully view the work being examined.

prompt: Do I need a permit to build a fence in Toronto?
answer:
In Toronto a **regular residential fence** (e.g., a garden or yard fence) **does not require a building permit**. * **Comply with the Zoning By‑law** (set‑backs, height limits, etc.). Even when a building permit isn’t required, the Zoning By‑law applies to all fences【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/9273-Building-Permit-Guide-WEB.pdf】.

**Bottom line:**  
- A typical backyard fence does **not** need a building permit.  
- A pool fence enclosure **does** need a permit.  
- Any work that impacts the public right‑of‑way, heritage properties, or other special circumstances may require additional permits.  

If you’re unsure about height limits or setbacks for your specific lot, you can contact Toronto Building at 416‑397‑5330 or review the Zoning By‑law details on the City’s website.

prompt: What is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto?
answer:
# Building Permit Application Process in Toronto

Based on the provided evidence, here is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto:

## General Steps in the Permitting Process

The permitting process generally has five steps:

1. **Determining if your project complies with zoning and applicable laws**
2. **Drafting your own plans or hiring a qualified designer** to prepare your application and drawings
3. **Applying for a building permit application** to the City of Toronto and obtaining a permit
4. **Starting construction and calling for your inspections**
5. **Closing your permit by calling for your final inspection**

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/9273-Building-Permit-Guide-WEB.pdf]

---

## Detailed Application Process

### 1. Prepare Your Application
Prepare your application using the **Building Permit Application Guides**, which outline required documentation, forms, and fees. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

### 2. Submit Your Application
Submit your application and all required documents and forms to:
- **Email:** bldapplications@toronto.ca, or
- **Online:** Toronto Building Intake Portal

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

### 3. Initial Review (Within One Business Day)
City staff will review your submission within one business day to determine if it is sufficient. You will receive a **Submission Status Letter** by email that either:
- **Finds the application sufficient:** Requests payment of initial fees (payable by credit card over the phone). A Plan Examiner is then assigned for a full review.
- **Finds the application insufficient:** Lists additional items required before a review can start.

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

### 4. Plan Review Process
Once a sufficient application is received, staff undertake a thorough review for compliance, which may include:
- **Zoning Review** – confirms compliance with the Zoning By-law and applicable laws
- **Building Code Review** – reviews plans for compliance with the Ontario Building Code
- **Mechanical Plans Examination** (if applicable) – reviews HVAC, plumbing, drainage, and private sewage systems
- **Fire Prevention Examination** (if applicable) – for certain multi-family residential, commercial, industrial, and institutional applications

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/]

### 5. Permit Issuance
Once your application has been reviewed and found to comply with building regulations, and you have paid all required fees, your permit will be **issued electronically**. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

### 6. Begin Construction & Schedule Inspections
After receiving your permit, you may begin work. You are required to schedule a **final inspection** upon completion to close the permit. Inspections may be requested online using the Toronto Building Inspection Requests web app. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

---

## Tips for a Smooth Application
- Apply as early as possible
- Ensure your application is complete (missing requirements are the most common cause of delays)
- Include the zoning declaration and tree declaration forms
- Confirm all forms are signed and your project is designed by a qualified professional when required
- Submit high-quality, properly formatted drawings (sketches are not accepted); all drawings must be flattened and combined in a single PDF

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

Express Services is an enhanced Building Permit service for certain types of smaller, less complex projects within a predefined scope. - Part 9 houses with not more than two dwelling units (no active building permit for new residential building or addition)

- Interior alterations to Business, Office, Retail Uses and Restaurants with less than 30 seats (Group D & E Occupancies) – up to 600 square metres, no change in use or patron area
- Tents (including certified tents)
- Minor fire damage repair
- Stand-alone maglocks
- Solar panel installations attached to an existing building

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

**Sign Permits:**
- First Party Signs (up to 3 signs)

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/express-building-permits/]

- Projects requiring Heritage Approval

- Revisions to permits for projects that included work outside the scope of Express Services

prompt: What happens if I build without a permit in Toronto?
answer:
If you start construction work without a required building permit in Toronto, you could face serious and potentially costly consequences, including:

**1. "Work Without Permit" Administrative Fee**
This is an additional fee equal to 50 percent of the permit fees for the project. The fee has a minimum and maximum value that is updated periodically. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**2. Delays**
All work must stop while your permit application is processed. The original timeline and fees to process an application still apply. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**3. Possible Undoing of Work**
You may have to undo the work that was already done. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**4. Additional Unplanned Work**
You may have to do more work than you originally planned and budgeted for, such as additional structural or mechanical work. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**5. Legal and Financial Issues**
You could face possible legal and/or financial issues down the road, such as impacts on selling your property or making an insurance claim. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**Important Note:** As the homeowner, you are responsible for paying these fees or penalties yourself even if you have hired a contractor who assured you that permits were not needed. Specifically, if you do not have a permit for work that has already started and it turns out you need one, you could face the following:

*   **Administrative Fee:** You will be charged a "work without permit" administrative fee equal to 50 percent of the permit fees for the project [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].

*   **Additional Work:** You may have to do more work than originally planned and budgeted for, such as additional structural or mechanical work [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
*   **Legal and Financial Issues:** You may encounter legal and/or financial issues down the road, such as difficulties selling your property or making an insurance claim [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/].
*   **Enforcement Measures:** Property owners who fail to comply may face progressive enforcement measures, including legal action [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/closing-building-permits/].

prompt: What is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto?
answer:
The process for applying for a building permit in Toronto generally involves the following steps:

**1. Preparation and Planning**
First, determine if your project complies with zoning and applicable laws. You must draft your own plans or hire a qualified designer to prepare your application and drawings. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/9273-Building-Permit-Guide-WEB.pdf]

**2. Submit Your Application**
Prepare your application using the Building Permit Application Guides and submit all required documents and forms to **bldapplications@toronto.ca** or online using the Toronto Building Intake Portal. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

**3. Initial Sufficiency Review**
City staff will review your submission within one business day to determine if it is sufficient to make an application. You will receive a Submission Status Letter by email that either:
- Finds the application sufficient and requests payment of initial fees (which can be paid by telephone via credit card), after which a Plan Examiner is assigned
- Finds the application insufficient and lists the additional items required before a review can start [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

**4. Plan Review Process**
Once your application is deemed sufficient, staff undertake a thorough review for compliance with:
- **Zoning Review**: Verification of compliance with the Zoning By-law regarding land use, building size, location, lot dimensions, parking, and height, plus applicable laws (Conservation Authorities Act, Planning Act, etc.)
- **Building Code Review**: Review of plans for compliance with health and safety, fire protection, structural sufficiency, construction materials, and plumbing/mechanical systems
- **Mechanical Plans Examination** (if applicable): Review of HVAC, plumbing, drainage and sewage systems
- **Fire Prevention Examination** (if applicable): For multi-family residential, commercial, industrial and institutional applications with fire protection systems [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/]

**5. Permit Issuance**
Once your application is reviewed and found to comply with building regulations, and you have paid all required fees, your permit will be issued electronically. If additional fees are required, you will be notified by email and must pay before issuance. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

**6. Construction and Inspections**
Once you have received your permit, you may begin work. You must schedule inspections during construction and a final inspection upon completion to close the permit. Inspections may be requested online using the Toronto Building Inspection Requests web app. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

**Important Tips:**
- Apply as early as possible, as back-and-forth may be required to ensure documents satisfy requirements
- Include zoning declaration and tree declaration forms (frequently overlooked)
- Ensure all forms are signed and projects are designed by qualified professionals when required (for new construction, structural changes, or additions)
- Submit high-quality, properly formatted drawings in a single PDF—sketches are not accepted [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

- Excavating and/or constructing foundations
- Basement underpinning

prompt: What happens if I build without a permit in Toronto?
answer:
If you build without a required permit in Toronto, you could face serious and potentially costly consequences, including:

**Financial Penalties and Fees**
- A "work without permit" administrative fee equal to **50 percent of the permit fees** for the project (subject to minimum and maximum values that are updated periodically) [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**Construction Delays**
- A delay while your permit application is processed, during which **all work must stop**. The original timeline and fees to process an application still apply [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**Remediation Requirements**
- Possibly having to **undo the work** that was done [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]
- Possibly having to **do more work than originally planned**, such as additional structural or mechanical work [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

**Legal and Financial Risks**
- Possible legal and/or financial issues down the road, such as **impacts on selling your property** or **making an insurance claim** [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]
- Property owners who fail to comply may face **progressive enforcement measures, including legal action** [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/closing-building-permits/]

**Important Note on Responsibility**
As the homeowner, you are responsible for paying these fees or penalties yourself **even if you have hired a contractor who assured you that permits were not needed** [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/working-without-a-permit/]

A laneway suite is a self-contained residential unit located on the same lot as a detached house, semi-detached house or townhouse, generally located in the rear yard next to a laneway [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/].

If drawings were prepared by a qualified designer (as defined under Div. C, Part 3, Section 3.2 of the Ontario Building Code), drawings must include the designer's name, registration number, qualification identification number, signature, and stamp/statement that the person has reviewed and taken responsibility for the design activities [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/].

**Required Documentation**
You must provide:
- **Floor Plans**: Fully dimensioned, for each level showing existing and proposed uses of all spaces, including location of smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detectors, and all plumbing fixtures. **Firefighting Access Requirements**
All laneway suites must be provided with principal access as per the Ontario Building Code (Div. B. 9.9.2.4.) and fire access as per (Div. B. 9.10.20.3) [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/].
